title: General Divisibility Rule Existence for Any d Coprime to 10
description: Proves that for every d > 1 coprime to 10, there exists k > 0 such that d ∣ n ↔ d ∣ (sum of digits of n in base 10^k). The witness k = φ(d) is given by Euler's theorem: 10^φ(d) ≡ 1 (mod d). This generalizes the parent proof's specific divisibility rules (d = 3, 9, 11, 37, ...) to all d coprime to 10.

overview.historicalContext:
Divisibility rules by digit sums have a long history. The rule for 9 ('cast out nines') was known in ancient and medieval mathematics — it appears in writings attributed to the Arab mathematician al-Uqlidisi (c. 950 AD) and was standard in European arithmetic by the 13th century. The rule for 11 (alternating digit sum) was described by Fibonacci in the Liber Abaci (1202). Rules for other moduli were studied systematically in the 17th–19th centuries as modular arithmetic developed.

The theoretical framework unifying these rules comes from Euler's totient theorem (Euler, 1763): for any d with gcd(a, d) = 1, a^φ(d) ≡ 1 (mod d). Taking a = 10, this gives 10^φ(d) ≡ 1 (mod d) for any d coprime to 10 — precisely the condition needed for a digit-block rule with block length k = φ(d). The optimal block length is the multiplicative order ord_d(10), which divides φ(d) by Lagrange's theorem in the group (ℤ/dℤ)×.

This formalization (OQ-01) answers the open question from the parent proof: the existence of a digit-block rule is guaranteed for every d coprime to 10, not just for d = 3, 9, 11, 37. The proof is entirely machine-verified using Euler's theorem from Mathlib (ZMod.pow_totient).
overview.problemStatement: Prove that for every d > 1 with gcd(d, 10) = 1, there exists k > 0 such that for all n ∈ ℕ, d ∣ n ↔ d ∣ (Nat.digits (10^k) n).sum.
overview.text: For any d > 1 coprime to 10, a digit-block sum divisibility rule exists, with witness k = φ(d).
overview.proofStrategy: By Euler's theorem (ZMod.pow_totient), the element 10 (as a unit in (ZMod d)ˣ via ZMod.unitOfCoprime) satisfies 10^φ(d) = 1 in ZMod d. Converting via ZMod.natCast_eq_natCast_iff gives 10^φ(d) ≡ 1 (mod d). Then Nat.modEq_digits_sum gives n ≡ (digits(10^k, n)).sum (mod d), and Nat.ModEq.dvd_iff converts this to the divisibility equivalence.
keyInsights: Euler's theorem gives 10^φ(d) ≡ 1 (mod d) for any d coprime to 10
ZMod.unitOfCoprime constructs 10 as a unit in (ZMod d)ˣ when gcd(d,10)=1
Nat.modEq_digits_sum connects the congruence 10^k ≡ 1 (mod d) to a digit sum rule
The optimal k is the multiplicative order ord_d(10), which divides φ(d); using k=φ(d) is sufficient
Concrete witnesses: d=3→k=1, d=7→k=6, d=11→k=2, d=13→k=6, d=37→k=3, d=41→k=5

sections.title: ZMod Unit Construction and Euler's Theorem
sections.summary: Constructs the NeZero instance, builds u = ZMod.unitOfCoprime 10 hcop.symm, applies ZMod.pow_totient to get u^φ(d) = 1, and coerces through Units.val to get (10 : ZMod d)^φ(d) = 1.
sections.mathContext: The group (ZMod d)ˣ has order φ(d) by Euler's theorem. `ZMod.unitOfCoprime 10 hcop.symm` constructs 10 as a unit when gcd(10, d) = 1. `ZMod.pow_totient u` gives u^φ(d) = 1 in (ZMod d)ˣ. `congr_arg Units.val` extracts the underlying ZMod d element: (u : ZMod d)^φ(d) = 1.

sections.title: Casting Back to ℕ Arithmetic
sections.summary: Casts (10 : ZMod d)^φ(d) = 1 back to a ℕ congruence using ZMod.natCast_eq_natCast_iff, then simplifies 1 % d = 1 via Nat.mod_eq_of_lt hd to conclude 10^φ(d) % d = 1.
sections.mathContext: `ZMod.natCast_eq_natCast_iff` bridges ZMod equality and ℕ modular congruence: (a : ZMod d) = (b : ZMod d) ↔ a ≡ b [MOD d]. With a = 10^φ(d), b = 1: the ZMod identity rewrites to Nat.ModEq, then `Nat.mod_eq_of_lt hd` gives 1 % d = 1 (since 1 < d), yielding 10^φ(d) % d = 1.

sections.title: Main Existence Theorem via φ(d) Witness
sections.summary: Proves general_divisibility_rule_exists: refine provides witness k = φ(d) with 0 < φ(d) from Nat.totient_pos. The inner goal d ∣ n ↔ d ∣ (digits(10^k,n)).sum is closed by Nat.ModEq.dvd_iff applied to Nat.modEq_digits_sum.
sections.mathContext: `Nat.modEq_digits_sum d b hb n` states: if b ≡ 1 (mod d), then n ≡ (Nat.digits b n).sum (mod d). With b = 10^φ(d) and hb = ten_pow_totient_mod_eq_one, this gives n ≡ digit-sum (mod d). `Nat.ModEq.dvd_iff` converts: n ≡ m [MOD d] → (d ∣ n ↔ d ∣ m).

sections.title: Concrete Witnesses: d = 3, 7, 11
sections.summary: Three well-known divisibility rules: d=3 with k=1 (digit sum rule: 3∣n ↔ 3∣digit-sum), d=7 with k=6 (six-digit block sum: 7∣n ↔ 7∣(block sum in base 10^6)), d=11 with k=2 (two-digit block sum: 11∣n ↔ 11∣(two-digit block sum)).
sections.mathContext: For d=3: 10 ≡ 1 (mod 3), so k=1 = ord_3(10) = φ(3) = 2? No — φ(3)=2 but ord_3(10)=1; k=1 is optimal. For d=7: 10^6 ≡ 1 (mod 7) and ord_7(10)=6 = φ(7), so k=6 is both optimal and equal to φ(7). For d=11: 100 ≡ 1 (mod 11) and ord_11(10)=2 < φ(11)=10; k=2 is optimal. Each checked via `native_decide`.

sections.title: Concrete Witnesses: d = 13, 37, 41
sections.summary: Three cases where the optimal k is much smaller than φ(d): d=13 with k=6 (ord_13(10)=6 vs φ(13)=12), d=37 with k=3 (ord_37(10)=3 vs φ(37)=36), d=41 with k=5 (ord_41(10)=5 vs φ(41)=40).
sections.mathContext: The multiplicative order ord_d(10) divides φ(d) by Lagrange's theorem. For d=37: 10^3 = 1000 ≡ 1 (mod 37) (since 1000 = 27·37 + 1). This gives the three-digit block rule: 37∣n ↔ 37∣(three-digit blocks sum). For d=41: 10^5 = 100000 ≡ 1 (mod 41) (since 100000 = 2439·41 + 1). These show the witness k=φ(d) in the existence theorem is sufficient but not minimal — ord_d(10) is the true optimal.

crossReferences.description: Answers the open question: does a digit-block divisibility rule exist for ALL d coprime to 10?

conclusion.summary: A complete proof that every d > 1 coprime to 10 admits a digit-block divisibility rule, with k = φ(d) as an explicit universal witness. 0 sorries, 0 axioms.
conclusion.implications: Provides the theoretical foundation for algorithmic divisibility testing of any number coprime to 10 using positional digit sums.
openQuestions: What is the minimal k for a given d? (Equals the multiplicative order ord_d(10), which can be computed.)
Can the rule be extended to bases other than 10? (Yes: replace 10 with any base b and take k = ord_d(b).)
